title: Atomic Edge Resonators Flatten Phonon Bands in Biphenylene Nanoribbons
authors: V. L. Katkov, N. M. Chtchelkatchev, V. A. Osipov
abstract: We show that H--F edge complexes in biphenylene nanoribbons act as intrinsic atomic resonators, flattening low-frequency phonon branches. With increasing wave vector, flexural and twisting vibrations concentrate at the edges while motion of the carbon backbone is suppressed. Displacement profiles and edge-mass tuning identify a local-resonance mechanism, an atomic counterpart of a tuned mass damper. Combining machine-learned interatomic potentials, frozen-phonon calculations, and density-functional tight binding, we find that weakly dispersive modes contribute substantially to thermal band-gap narrowing. Zero-point motion shifts the calculated gap closure toward the experimentally observed ribbon widths. A hexagonal boron nitride substrate preserves the principal spectral features while reducing thermal renormalization. These results establish edge chemistry as a route to nearly flat phonon bands and connect a local atomic resonance to the electronic response of an entire nanoribbon.
summary: This work demonstrates that the atomic structure at the edges of biphenylene nanoribbons can act as intrinsic resonators, flattening specific phonon branches. This localized vibrational resonance mechanism is shown to significantly influence the electronic band gap, particularly under thermal excitation. The findings establish edge chemistry as a powerful, controllable route for tailoring the electronic properties of carbon nanostructures.
main_problem: The study investigates how controlling atomic edge chemistry can manipulate the collective vibrational modes (phonons) in nanoribbons and consequently alter their electronic band structure.
main_result: H–F edge complexes act as intrinsic atomic resonators, causing low-frequency phonon bands to flatten, which contributes to thermal band-gap narrowing in the nanoribbon.
method: The research employs a combination of machine-learned interatomic potentials, frozen-phonon calculations, and density-functional tight binding to model phonon dispersion and electronic response.
model_or_system: The physical system is biphenylene nanoribbons, analyzed both freestanding and supported on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), with the focus on the role of H–F edge complexes.
key_observables: Phonon bands, electronic band gap ($E_g$), signed gap-response spectrum ($g_{2F}(\omega)$), and mode eigenvectors (WBM, TW, ZA).
important_parameters: Wave vector ($q$), ribbon width ($N_h$), and temperature ($T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on harmonic gap analysis and approximations for gap renormalization, though the edge resonance mechanism is linked to local atomic dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate width-dependent band gaps (static vs. zero-point renormalized), thermal band-edge shifts, and the signed gap-response spectrum, mapping spectral features to specific vibrational modes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the role of edge complexes as resonators, quantifying the resulting phonon band flattening via mode analysis, and finally connecting this vibrational control to measurable electronic properties like gap narrowing.
why_interesting: The concept of using engineered atomic structures (edge chemistry) to engineer collective excitations (phonons) and thereby tune electronic properties is highly relevant to designing novel quantum materials and nano-devices.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Thermal band-edge shift ∆Eg(T) = Eg(T) −Eg(0) for (a) freestanding and (b) hBN-supported ribbons. Colors identify Nh. The reference Eg(0) includes zero-point renor- malization. For Nh = 7, 8, the curves track the change in band-edge separation after gap closure, rather than a finite insulating gap.

Figure 1. Width-dependent band gap. Red and gold curves show the present static-lattice and zero-point-renormalized results, respectively. Black solid and dashed curves are ex- periment and DFT from Ref. 14; black dash-dotted and blue curves are DFT from Ref. 16 and earlier DFTB results [17]. The inset defines Nh for a ribbon with Nh = 4.

Figure 4. (a) Phonon spectrum of a freestanding ribbon with Nh = 5, calculated within the tight-binding approxi- mation. The colored branches determine features A and B of the spectral function g2F(ω). (b)–(e) Displacement patterns of selected modes at the indicated values of q: WBM is the width-breathing mode, TW is the twisting mode, and ZA is the flexural acoustic mode. The displacement amplitudes are magnified for clarity.

Figure 3. Signed gap-response spectrum g2F(ω) [Eq. (3)] for (a) freestanding and (b) hBN-supported ribbons. A and B mark the low-frequency and width-dependent groups of fea- tures. Colors label Nh. Frequencies are shown as ℏω/kB, with Gaussian broadening σ = 23 K.

Figure 5. Normalized transverse profiles of the atomic dis- placement amplitudes An(q) for the TW (a) and ZA (b) branches of a freestanding ribbon with Nh = 5. The index n labels the atomic rows across the ribbon, and color denotes the wave vector q. The value qc corresponds to the crossover from motion distributed across the ribbon width to predomi- nantly edge-localized motion.
